title: Judge C: AI and agents researcher judge
brief:
You are a judge for the PayPal AI Hackathon on Devpost (2026). Your background: applied AI researcher working on LLM agents, agentic commerce protocols (AP2, MCP, A2A) and agent safety. You are skeptical of buzzwords and check whether "AI" is meaningful. Judge the project "Join" strictly and fairly. Do not edit any files.

Official judging (Rules §6):
- Stage One (pass/fail): "reasonably fits the theme and reasonably applies the required APIs/SDKs" (an app that integrates the PayPal developer platform, sandbox, along with an AI tool, model, or platform).
- Stage Two: five criteria of EQUAL weight, each 1-10: Technological Implementation, Design, Potential Impact, Innovation (quality of the idea), Presentation. Ties break on Technological Implementation first.
- Honorable mentions include "Best Use of PayPal + AI" and "Best Use of Agentic Commerce". The demo video is NOT recorded yet; score Presentation as it stands.

Materials (read and verify; don't trust the team's claims):
- The repository at D:\paypal\join: README.md, docs/SUBMISSION.md, docs/JUDGING.md, docs/TECHNICAL.md, docs/NEGOTIATION.md.
- Code: api/src/mcp.js, api/src/ops.js, api/src/negotiate/engine.js, api/src/mandate.js, api/src/proof/mandates.js (AP2), api/src/proof/tlog.js and receipts.js, api/src/auth.js, api/src/scout/understand.js (the website agent's Qwen use), api/src/reviews.js, web/src/scout/agent.js, web/src/webmcp.js, examples/*.mjs, api/bench/negotiation.mjs, api/test/*.
- You may run `npm test` in D:\paypal\join\api and `node bench/negotiation.mjs` there (both offline, in memory). Don't change anything.
Questions to answer for yourself: How much real AI is there, and where (the person's own agent via MCP/A2A, Qwen 0.5B on the server, rules)? Is the agent safety story (mandates, scopes, signed requests, tool fingerprint, limits enforced in code) real and correct? Are AP2 and the transparency log implemented faithfully or decorative? Does the negotiation benchmark show something meaningful?

Report (concise, plain text):
1. Stage One: pass/fail and why.
2. For each of the five criteria: score 1-10, strongest evidence (file paths), biggest weaknesses.
3. Total out of 50; whether it is a credible contender for "Best Use of Agentic Commerce" or "Best Use of PayPal + AI", and why.
4. Any claim in the docs you found overstated or wrong (quote it).
5. The three changes that would raise your scores most before Nov 12, with criterion and rough effect.
Be specific and critical.

# Negotiation: the venue's rules, and a benchmark

Every venue on Join sets its own negotiation policy (`api/data/world.json`, editable in Venue view): a list price,
off-peak, group and last-minute discounts, a style (`firm`, `standard` or `eager`), a number of counter-offers, and a
floor that is never revealed. Join's engine (`api/src/negotiate/engine.js`) enforces it for every agent alike.

- **A schedule, not a haggle with a model.** Each serious offer moves the venue one step down its own concession
  schedule, from its opening ask toward its floor (`standard` goes half way, `eager` all the way, `firm` not at all).
  An offer at or above the next step is accepted.
- **Lowballs don't move it.** An offer under 70% of the current ask uses up a round and the venue doesn't come down.
- **Best and final.** After the last counter (or at once for a `firm` venue) the price is final; an offer under a final
  price ends the negotiation.
- **No floor-finding.** Five negotiations per person, venue and day; the floor is never sent to an agent.

## Benchmark

`node api/bench/negotiation.mjs --md` plays six buyer strategies against every venue, activity and two start times
(28 negotiations each) on the real engine, in memory, with no limits in the way. Prices are the share of the venue's
opening ask, of its list price, and of its secret floor.

| strategy | runs | deals | paid / opening ask | paid / list | paid / floor (min) | rounds | under floor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Accept the opening ask | 28 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 88.0% | 107.3% (100.0%) | 0.0 | 0 |
| Conceder (offers 90%, takes the first counter) | 28 | 67.9% | 97.9% | 84.6% | 108.1% (100.0%) | 1.0 | 0 |
| Split the difference (85%, then halfway) | 28 | 67.9% | 95.7% | 82.7% | 105.6% (100.0%) | 1.8 | 0 |
| Patient (Join's buyer: just over 70% each round, takes the final) | 28 | 100.0% | 95.7% | 84.1% | 101.9% (100.0%) | 1.5 | 0 |
| Lowballer (30% every round) | 28 | 100.0% | 100.0% | 88.0% | 107.3% (100.0%) | 1.5 | 0 |
| Floor prober (binary search, then accepts) | 28 | 100.0% | 97.2% | 85.5% | 103.8% (100.0%) | 1.5 | 0 |

Time waster: 5 negotiations opened with one venue on one day, then refused (`quota`).

**What it shows.**
- **No strategy ever paid under a floor**, and lowballing saves nothing: the lowballer paid the full opening ask.
- **Patience wins.** The patient buyer (Join's website agent: just over 70% of the ask each round, never an offer once
  the price is final, then the final price) got a deal every time and the lowest price of the strategies that always
  got one. This matches recent work on LLM bargaining, where aggressive anchoring, calibrated concessions and patience
  did best and fast conceders did worst (Bergemann et al., *Training Language Models for Bilateral Trade with Private
  Information*, arXiv 2604.16472, 2026).
- **Conceding early loses deals, not only money.** "Offer 90%, take the counter" and "split the difference" lost a

**Judge's report on "Join"**

I ran `npm test` (46 of 46 pass) and `node bench/negotiation.mjs` (output matches docs/NEGOTIATION.md). I read the code you listed. I did not run the live sandbox, Ollama or Claude examples.

**Where the AI is**
- **The person's own agent over MCP/A2A.** This is the only real LLM, and it is external. Join contains no agent loop. `examples/claude-agent.mjs` is the sole LLM client, and the docs admit it was never run (no key).
- **Qwen2.5-0.5B on Join's server.** It is a one-slot activity classifier, called only when the regex rules find no activity (`api/src/scout/understand.js`). Its only test is against a stub Ollama. The docs report a manual check of 15 messages with one miss.
- **Everything else is rules.** Intent parsing, the website agent (`web/src/scout/agent.js`: offers 72% of the ask, then takes the final price), venue pricing and concession schedules are all fixed code. The venue is not an agent.

## 1. Stage One: PASS
- The PayPal side is deep and mostly sandbox-verified: Orders AUTHORIZE, partial capture, void, refund, Payouts, Vault, Invoicing, SDK v6 and Agent Toolkit calls.
- The AI side is thin but real: MCP/A2A endpoints for outside LLM agents, Qwen in the loop, and the PayPal Agent Toolkit. "Reasonably applies" is satisfied, though weakly on the AI half.

## 2. Stage Two

**Technological Implementation: 8/10**
- **Strengths.**
  - `api/src/pay/settle.js` has an idempotent settlement state machine and a guarantee-then-partial-capture design.
  - `api/src/proof/tlog.js` is a faithful RFC 6962/9162 implementation: inclusion and consistency verification follow the RFC algorithms, C2SP notes use correct key IDs, and cosignatures use type 0x04 over `cosignature/v1`. It is not decorative.
  - Scoped tokens and the RFC 9421 verifier in `auth.js` are correct (method, authority, path and content-digest are covered, there is a 5-minute window, and tests cover tamper, wrong key and wrong host).
  - Limits are enforced in code. `engine.js` `overMandate` runs before the venue sees an offer, and `settle.js` applies `fits` and `coverFits` on every payment path.
  - The tool-description digest at `/.well-known/mcp-tools.json` is a good anti-rug-pull idea. I did not verify that any client example actually pins it.
- **Weaknesses.**
  - AP2 is an export layer, not an enforcement layer. The JWS mandates in `proof/mandates.js` are issued but never verified on use. Enforcement reads the plain JSON store (`getMandate`).
  - `cnf.kid` is a token id, not a public key, so there is no proof of possession.
  - Join is both issuer and verifier. Docs §13.0 concedes this.
  - There is a units bug inside one mandate: `payment.amount_range.max = m.perGame` is in cents (5000), while `payment.budget.max = perWeek/100` is in dollars (200). `ap2.test.js` asserts both values.
  - `verify()` ignores `exp`.
  - The tlog has a single operator and a single witness in the demo, and no gossip.
  - There is no replay nonce on signed requests within the 5-minute window.
  - State is JSON files and in-memory sessions.

**Design: 7/10**
- **Strengths.**
  - The Activity page is a human-readable audit trail of agent steps built from facts (`api/src/activity.js`).
  - The no-agent drawer works in English and Chinese.
  - The demo panel plays the friends so one window shows the whole group.
  - The negotiation curve chart is a clear visual.
  - The receipt verifies in the browser.
- **Weaknesses.**
  - Demo-world only: 10 venues, regex-parsed intents.
  - The docs describe dense mechanisms (tlog, AP2) that ordinary users never need to see.

**Potential Impact: 6/10**
- Group-plan payment friction is real, and the sprawl of PayPal surfaces is good for PayPal. The invoice and payout fallbacks for non-payers are genuinely useful.
- Weaknesses:
  - The venue side is a simulated policy engine, with no actual venue adoption path.
  - Join holds the funds because multiparty onboarding isn't available. That is a compliance and marketplace …(+4259 chars)
